lines: In nineteen twenty-two, Charles {Osborne|AA1 Z B AO0 R N} was working on a farm in {Nebraska|N AH0 B R AE1 S K AH0}, hanging a three hundred and fifty pound hog.
He fell, but felt nothing at the time. [pause 120] Then the hiccups started.
They did not stop for *sixty-eight years*.
Under your lungs is a dome of muscle called the {diaphragm|D AY1 AH0 F R AE0 M}. It pulls down each time you breathe in.
In a hiccup, it twitches on its own, and air rushes in.
A split second later, your vocal cords snap shut. [pause 100] That snap is the *hic*.
It is a reflex. Nerves carry the signal up to your {brainstem|B R EY1 N S T EH0 M}, and back down to the {diaphragm|D AY1 AH0 F R AE0 M}.
One idea: [pause 100] his fall damaged a tiny spot in his {brainstem|B R EY1 N S T EH0 M} that normally switches hiccups *off*.
He {hiccuped|HH IH1 K AH0 P T} twenty to forty times a minute, an estimated four hundred and thirty million times.
He still married twice, had eight children, and later blended his meals.
In nineteen ninety, the hiccups stopped. [pause 150] Nobody knows why.
Most hiccups stop within minutes. If they last more than two days, see a doctor.
